title: Urban resilience is shifting from post-disaster response toward risk-informed spatial planning that governs where growth, housing, services and infrastructure can safely occur
source_unit: World Bank, Handbook for Livable and Resilient Cities: Integrating Hazard and Risk Information into Urban Planning
geography: Global urban-planning framework with examples and guidance for national and local governments, especially in rapidly urbanizing and emerging-economy contexts

observations.period: 2026 handbook; definition of livable and resilient urban development

livability_bundle.value: green and resilient growth, social inclusion, resilient built environments and shared prosperity

access_bundle.value: healthy environments, affordable housing, essential services, jobs, and low-carbon transportation and economies
access_bundle.unit: reported access conditions for livable cities

risk_scope.value: urban risk is shaped by the interaction of hazards, exposure, vulnerability, infrastructure, ecosystems and governance

observations.method: World Bank conceptual and operational handbook synthesizing urbanization, hazard, climate, spatial-planning, infrastructure, governance and resilience practice.
observations.uncertainty: The framework identifies conditions and planning routes rather than estimating one global effect of risk-informed planning on safety, mobility, health or economic opportunity.
observations.subgroup: Urban residents, low-income households, informal-settlement residents, local governments, planners, infrastructure providers, employers and communities exposed to climate and disaster risks.
observations.counterinterpretation: Urban growth can reduce risk through density, proximity, services and economic opportunity when governance and infrastructure keep pace; risk is not an inevitable consequence of urbanization.

observations.period: 2026 handbook; risk-informed spatial planning and development control

restrict.value: restrict development in high-hazard or unacceptable-risk areas and preserve zones for protection, buffers or ecosystem functions

condition.value: condition development on risk studies and measures such as elevation, structural reinforcement, drainage control or hazard-specific standards

promote.value: promote growth toward safer areas through public investment, incentives and nature-based solutions

planning_shift.value: risk data should guide zoning, infrastructure siting and investment before disasters occur

observations.method: Handbook operational framework translating hazard and risk information into land-use rules, investment priorities and development standards.
observations.uncertainty: The RCP framework is a planning model; implementation depends on land administration, enforcement, finance, political authority, compensation, participation and the quality of hazard data.
observations.subgroup: Residents and landholders in hazard-prone areas, informal settlements, developers, infrastructure agencies, planners, elected officials and affected communities.
observations.counterinterpretation: Restrictions or relocation can impose costs, disrupt livelihoods and reproduce exclusion if safer land, housing, transport, services and participation are not provided.

data_capacity.value: many cities, especially in emerging economies, lack the data systems and institutional capacity to translate hazard information into planning decisions

multi_level_governance.value: effective risk-informed planning requires coordination among urban planners, disaster-risk managers, climate-risk managers and multiple levels of government

implementation_cycle.value: context diagnosis, plan formulation, implementation, monitoring and evaluation should be linked as a continuous planning cycle

participation.value: governance, community participation and accountability are part of the enabling environment for enforceable risk-informed plans

observations.method: World Bank guidance on enabling environments, risk assessment, plan formulation, implementation, enforcement, monitoring and evaluation.
observations.uncertainty: The handbook illustrates tools and cases but does not provide a comparable global score of city capacity, enforcement or participation quality.
observations.subgroup: Local and national public agencies, communities, civil society, technical experts, private investors and residents whose land, mobility or livelihoods are affected by planning decisions.
observations.counterinterpretation: More data and coordination do not guarantee fair outcomes; technical planning can still obscure distributional trade-offs, land politics or community knowledge unless accountability is real.

related_sources.claim: Official World Bank document record for the handbook.
GFDRR publication context for the City Resilience Program and risk-informed urban planning.

boundary: This record adds a place-and-governance route: housing, services, mobility, infrastructure, risk data and climate exposure are joined through spatial planning and development control. It is a World Bank planning handbook, not a city-level outcome evaluation, household mobility study, property-market estimate, engineering certification or proof that participation and enforcement occur.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official World Bank document record, full handbook PDF and World Bank overview were retrieved and reviewed for livable-city conditions, risk-informed planning, the Restrict-Condition-Promote framework, institutional capacity, multi-level governance, participation and implementation; the PDF was hashed.
